name: Materialism and the state of nature as a 'war of all against all'
plain_explanation: Hobbes believed everything, including life and mind, is ultimately just matter in motion. Before any government exists, every person naturally desires both to preserve their own freedom and to gain power over others, and this clash of desires produces a constant war of all against all, making life 'nasty, brutish, and short,' with no property, justice, or injustice -- only force and fraud.
precise_definition: Russell's summary: 'Life, he says, is nothing but a motion of the limbs... In a state of nature, before there is any government, every man desires to preserve his own liberty, but to acquire dominion over others; both these desires are dictated by the impulse to self-preservation. From their conflict arises a war of all against all, which makes life "nasty, brutish, and short." In a state of nature, there is no property, no justice or injustice; there is only war, and "force and fraud are, in war, the two cardinal virtues."'
why_it_mattered: It supplies Hobbes's entire justification for government: since the state of nature is intolerable, rational self-interested individuals will consent to nearly any authority capable of ending it, which grounds his defense of near-absolute sovereignty.
historical_origin: Presented at the start of Leviathan (1651) as the foundation of Hobbes's political philosophy, notably unlike most defenders of despotic government in holding all men naturally equal.
examples: Hobbes's explicit denial that despotic government's defenders usually assume natural equality -- Hobbes does assume it
competing_positions: Aristotle's view of humans as naturally political/social animals capable of natural cooperation
influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly shaped, by contrast, Locke's and Rousseau's own versions of the social contract and state of nature, discussed later in Russell's book.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: This is the metaphysical and psychological foundation for Hobbes's entire political theory.
